label: Over-reduction
rule: NaBH₄ is a mild hydride: it reduces aldehydes and ketones only. It leaves C=C, esters and carboxylic acids alone. Reducing those needs LiAlH₄ (esters, acids) or H₂/Pt (C=C).

label: Stopped half-way
rule: LiAlH₄ does not stop at the aldehyde. The aldehyde formed from an ester or acid is more reactive than what you started with, so it is reduced again to the alcohol.

label: Ester kept in one piece
rule: LiAlH₄ attacks the ester carbonyl twice. After the first hydride the alkoxide leaves, so the ester splits: the acyl side becomes a 1° alcohol (RCH₂OH) and the alkoxy side becomes its own alcohol (R′OH). Never an ether, never one molecule.

label: HIO₄ gave alcohols
rule: HIO₄ cleaves the C–C bond between the two carbinol carbons of a vicinal diol and oxidises each to a carbonyl. The products are aldehydes and ketones, not alcohols.

label: -al vs -one
rule: Count carbon substituents on the carbonyl carbon: one carbon (plus H) is an aldehyde (-al, carbon 1); two carbons is a ketone (-one, needs a locant).

label: EAS replaced a substituent
rule: Three-step EAS check: (1) nothing already on the ring leaves, the new group replaces an H; (2) OH, OR and NH₂ direct ortho/para; (3) pick the open spots, and if para is blocked go ortho.

label: Para chosen when blocked
rule: If the para position already carries a group, the incoming group goes ortho to the directing OH. Check the ring for open positions before you draw.

label: O- vs C-acylation vs ether
rule: Without AlCl₃ an acid chloride or anhydride acylates the phenol OXYGEN (aryl ester). With AlCl₃ (or on an aryl ester, the Fries rearrangement) the acyl group goes on the RING o/p to OH (hydroxyaryl ketone), and the OH stays. NaOH/K₂CO₃ then an alkyl halide gives an ether, not an ester.

label: Wrong acyl group
rule: Keep the whole acyl group: RCO– from RCOCl keeps its C=O. Kolbe–Schmitt (NaOH, CO₂, pressure, then H₃O⁺) installs COOH ortho to OH, not CHO and not acetyl.

label: NaNO₂ is not nitration
rule: NaNO₂ + acid makes nitrous acid (HONO), which turns an Ar–NH₂ into Ar–N₂⁺ at 0–5 °C; H₂O and heat then put OH on that same carbon. Nitration needs HNO₃/H₂SO₄ and adds NO₂ to a ring C–H.

label: O₃ vs OsO₄
rule: OsO₄ (then NaHSO₃, or cat. OsO₄/NMO) adds two OH groups syn across the C=C and keeps the C–C bond: a diol. O₃ cleaves the C=C into two carbonyls.

label: Stereo left off
rule: When a reaction creates a new stereocenter from an achiral start you get both enantiomers: label it racemic. Syn additions to a symmetric cis-alkene give meso; to a trans-alkene racemic. Say it even when nobody asks.

label: Wrong stereo label
rule: Syn addition to a symmetric cis-alkene gives one compound with an internal mirror plane: meso. Syn addition to the trans isomer gives a pair of enantiomers: racemic. Draw it, then look for the mirror plane.

label: Regio reversed
rule: Hydroboration–oxidation (BH₃·THF then H₂O₂/NaOH) is anti-Markovnikov: the OH ends up on the less substituted carbon, syn to the H. Acid-catalysed additions put the nucleophile on the more substituted carbon.

label: Less substituted alkene
rule: Acid-catalysed dehydration (H₂SO₄, heat) is E1 and gives the Zaitsev product: the more substituted, more stable alkene is major.

label: Williamson with a 2°/3° halide
rule: Alkoxides are strong bases. With a 2° or 3° alkyl halide they do E2 and give the alkene, not the ether. Put the hindered group on the alkoxide and use a CH₃ or 1° halide (benzyl and allyl are great).

label: SN2 on an aryl carbon
rule: Backside attack is impossible on an sp² ring carbon, so aryl halides do not do SN2. An alkoxide only replaces an aryl halide by SNAr, and only when NO₂ is ortho or para to the halide.

label: Meta NO₂ treated as activating
rule: SNAr needs the negative charge of the Meisenheimer intermediate to reach the NO₂ group, which happens only from the ortho and para positions. A meta NO₂ does not help: no reaction.

label: AlCl₃ used as a base
rule: AlCl₃ is a Lewis acid; it cannot remove the O–H proton. To make the alkoxide for a Williamson ether synthesis use NaH, Na, NaOH or K₂CO₃ (for phenols).

label: Forgot the workup
rule: Hydride and Grignard additions give a metal alkoxide; the alcohol only appears after the H₂O or H₃O⁺ step. Diazonium salts only become phenols after H₂O and heat. Write the workup as its own step.

label: Steps out of order
rule: Order matters: make the nucleophile first (NaH, then the alkyl halide; RMgBr, then the carbonyl), and add the aqueous workup last. Water before a Grignard or hydride destroys it.

label: Wrong temperature or conditions
rule: Conditions change the product: diazotisation needs 0–5 °C or the diazonium salt decomposes; 1° alcohols with H₂SO₄ give the ether at 140 °C and the alkene at 180 °C; Kolbe–Schmitt needs CO₂ under pressure.

label: Epoxide regio reversed
rule: Anionic nucleophiles (RO⁻, CN⁻, N₃⁻, RS⁻, hydride, Grignard) open an epoxide at the LESS substituted carbon (SN2). Under acid (H₃O⁺, ROH/H₂SO₄, HX) the nucleophile attacks the MORE substituted carbon.

label: Inversion missing
rule: Epoxide opening is backside attack: the configuration at the attacked carbon inverts, and the new OH and nucleophile end up anti (trans on a ring).

label: Aryl–O bond broken
rule: Excess HBr or HI cleaves ethers to alkyl halides, but SN2 cannot happen at an sp² carbon. An alkyl aryl ether gives the phenol plus the alkyl halide; the aryl–O bond never breaks.

label: Wrong S oxidation level
rule: NaIO₄ stops at the sulfoxide. H₂O₂ or a peroxy acid gives the sulfoxide with 1 equivalent and the sulfone with 2 equivalents. Count the equivalents you poured.

label: Reagent not recognised
rule: Read the bottle: K₂CO₃ is a base for phenols, PhCH₂Br is benzyl bromide (a great SN2 electrophile), CH₃CO₂K is potassium acetate (an O-nucleophile with 18-crown-6). Open the reagent card to see what the tool does.

label: Locant missing or wrong
rule: Number the parent chain so the principal group (-ol, -al, -one) gets the lowest locant, and give every substituent a locant. Only aldehydes and carboxylic acids are allowed to drop their locant (it is always 1).

label: Substituents out of order
rule: List substituent prefixes alphabetically, ignoring di-/tri-/tetra- and italic prefixes like tert- and sec- (but not iso- or cyclo-).

label: '-oxide' used as an ether name
rule: 'Ethoxide' is the anion RO⁻. An ether is named as a functional-class name (groups alphabetically + 'ether': ethyl methyl ether) or substitutively (alkoxy + parent: methoxyethane).
